query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating advanced free‐energy sampling techniques (e.g., adaptive metadynamics and advanced thermodynamic integration) with calibration from selective in-situ neutron imaging will enable accurate and efficient determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high‐entropy alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy in its solid (or multiphase) state near its melting transition (e.g., systems such as CoCrCu approaching CoCrCuNi with added Ni).
generation.intervention: Apply enhanced free‐energy calculation methods within atomistic simulations; these methods will be calibrated using selective in-situ neutron imaging data from high-temperature experiments.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions near the melting point under controlled heating/cooling cycles, where both solid and liquid phases exist or transition rapidly.
generation.structural_mediator: The detailed free‐energy landscape of the high‐entropy alloy, capturing subtle free‐energy differences across multiphase states and complex liquid interactions.
generation.mechanism: Advanced sampling techniques effectively navigate the high-dimensional, complex free‐energy surfaces typical of multi-component alloys. Coupling these simulations with in-situ neutron imaging ensures that the simulation’s liquid-phase behavior and phase transitions are accurately calibrated, leading to precise predictions of melting temperature, latent heat (fusion enthalpy/entropy), and volume changes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated approach is expected to predict melting temperatures within approximately ±15 °C accuracy, capture fusion enthalpy and entropy within an approximate 10% error range, and determine volume changes in agreement with in-situ imaging observations across varied HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Conventional techniques (e.g., standard DSC, calorimetric methods, basic CALPHAD models) that have struggled with the resolution and efficiency required for the compositional complexity of HEAs.
generation.boundary: This method is applicable to HEA systems amenable to neutron imaging and where computational resources allow for enhanced free‐energy sampling; systems with extreme compositional or kinetic behaviors that fall outside the calibration window may require further adjustments.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative performance is influenced by alloy-specific interactions and potential calibration biases between simulation and experiment. The precise error margins may vary across different HEAs, necessitating further validation over a broader compositional space.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a systematic study where a series of high-entropy alloys are characterized both experimentally and via the enhanced free‐energy simulation approach. In experiments, utilize high-resolution neutron imaging and DSC under controlled heating/cooling cycles. In parallel, perform atomistic simulations using adaptive metadynamics or similar methods calibrated with the imaging data.
measurements: Melting temperature (°C) from both experiments and simulations
Fusion enthalpy (J/g or kJ/mol) and entropy (J/K·mol) determination
Volume change across melting (measured via imaging and simulation)
Liquid-phase mixing behavior and phase uniformity observed via neutron imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions deviate from the experimental measurements beyond the accepted thresholds (e.g., more than ±15 °C for melting temperature or over 10% error in fusion enthalpy/entropy) or if the predicted liquid-phase behavior (e.g., miscibility or phase separation) is inconsistent with the in-situ imaging data, then the proposed integrated approach is invalidated.

A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. Neutron imaging was simultaneously carried out to capture 10 radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back down to 1000 °C. This, in turn, produced a movie-like series of radiographs that allow for the observation of the buttons melting, the transition from immiscible to miscible as Ni is alloyed into the CoCrCu system, and solidification. In an effort to elucidate the liquid state behavior of high-entropy and related alloys, the present authors utilized the CG-1D Neutron Imaging Instrument at the High-Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory to image the melt separation process in-situ []. The technique utilizes a high-temperature furnace between a neutron beam and a detector, and was successfully implemented for the in-situ imaging of the liquid phase separation that occurs in equiatomic CoCrCu [] as this compound has been shown to exhibit a stable liquid phase separation into CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquids [,]. The experiment consisted of arc-melted CoCrCu buttons placed in a small alumina crucible inside a high-temperature vacuum furnace, which were then heated to 1500 °C, and slowly cooled back to room temperature with simultaneous neutron imaging being carried out in 25 °C steps. frame.system: High-entropy alloys comprising multiple principal elements that typically exhibit complex phase behavior near melting. The starting state is a solid (or multi-phase) high-entropy alloy approaching its melting transition.
frame.goal: To accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change during melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the entire high-entropy alloy family.
frame.limitation: Current techniques (e.g., conventional DSC, calorimetric and in-situ synchrotron methods, or computational thermodynamic models) often do not provide the needed accuracy and efficiency when confronted with the compositional complexity and diverse melting behaviors of high-entropy alloys.
constraints: Must state the physical rationale behind the approach
Expected quantitative performance (accuracy and efficiency metrics) should be detailed
The range of applicability across different compositions within the HEA family must be defined
Supporting prior evidence needs to be provided
A decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach if it fails must be specified
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions around the melting transition where both solid and liquid phases co-exist or transform. This involves dynamic environments such as rapid heating/cooling cycles or in-situ measurements under equilibrium/non-equilibrium conditions.
prior_attempts: Conventional differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) which may lack resolution or efficiency for complex, multi-component systems
In-situ synchrotron or X-ray diffraction methods that have been applied to limited alloy compositions but struggle with the full HEA compositional space
Computational thermodynamic models that often fall short in accurately representing the entropy and liquid-phase interactions in highly complex alloy systems

decision.trend: Over the past several years, research on high-entropy alloys has evolved from conventional bulk measurements and phase‐identification techniques toward in‐situ, real‐time imaging methods and computational phase evolution. Early works (e.g., those using DSC or synchrotron methods) struggled with the compositional complexity and rapid phase kinetics of HEAs during melting. The study using cold neutrons (PMC8320920) marked a significant advance by enabling direct, in‐situ observation of the liquid state and phase remixing, but it was limited in providing complete thermodynamic quantities (melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change, and liquid properties) over the entire HEA space. Concurrently, computational approaches (e.g., CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening and Monte Carlo simulations) have partly succeeded in predicting phase evolution but have not yet tackled the high-resolution free-energy landscape for the melting transition in these multi-principal element systems.
decision.unsolved: Despite the progress in experimental imaging and computational prediction, there remains a gap in accurately and efficiently obtaining the complete set of melting-related thermodynamic properties (i.e., melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and detailed liquid-phase behavior) for the entire high-entropy alloy family. In particular, capturing the complex liquid-phase interactions and the subtle free-energy differences in a computationally efficient manner remains unsolved.
decision.lever: Enhanced free-energy calculation methods (e.g., adaptive metadynamics or advanced thermodynamic integration) applied within atomistic simulations calibrated by selective in-situ imaging data
decision.why: Building on the trend that combined experimental in-situ imaging and high-throughput computational methods have each advanced our understanding but not fully resolved the melting thermodynamics, the next logical step is to deploy an enhanced sampling scheme. This lever precisely targets the free-energy landscape to robustly extract melting temperatures, latent heats, and volume changes across complex compositions. This approach leverages recent successes of free-energy methods in simpler systems and adapts them to account for the high-dimensional composition space and liquid-phase interactions characteristic of high-entropy alloys, thereby meeting the accuracy, efficiency, and validation criteria outlined in the research question.
